articles.title: The Cup That Saved the Camp
articles.dek: In 1971 a doctor in a flooded refugee camp ran out of the medicine everyone trusted. What he did next shows what the Bible's James meant by a faith that actually works.
articles.quote: Faith that stays in the heart saves no one; faith becomes life the moment it is poured into someone's cup.
articles.body:
In the summer of 1971, war drove millions of people out of what is now Bangladesh and across the border into India. At a camp near the town of Bangaon, the rains came, the latrines overflowed, and cholera moved through the crowded tents. Cholera is a brutal disease. A toxin made by the bacteria makes the intestine pour water out of the body, and a person can lose litres in a single day. Untreated, as many as a third of those infected may die, sometimes within hours.

The young doctor in charge was Dilip Mahalanabis. The standard treatment was intravenous saline, sterile salt water dripped straight into a vein. Within days, his team had run out of it. There were too many patients, too few needles, and too few trained hands. Mahalanabis made a decision that frightened some of his colleagues. He had his team mix ordinary table salt, glucose, and baking soda into clean water in large drums, and they handed it to the refugees in cups. Mothers spooned it into the mouths of their children. Fathers drank it and then fed their neighbors. Death rates in his camp fell to under four percent, while in other camps they stayed far higher.

The science behind those cups had been sitting in laboratories for about a decade. In 1960 a biochemist named Robert Crane described how the lining of the gut absorbs glucose: tiny gateways in the intestinal wall carry a molecule of sugar and atoms of sodium through together, and water follows them in. Cholera wrecks many of the body's systems, but it leaves that shared gateway working. Salt and sugar, taken together, can pull water back into a dying body faster than the disease drains it out. The medical journal The Lancet later called oral rehydration potentially the most important medical advance of the twentieth century. Yet for years the discovery lay in journals while children died of diarrhea. It saved no one until someone stirred it into water and put a cup into a trembling hand.

The letter of James was written for people who knew what they believed and needed to see what that belief was for. Its author is traditionally understood to be James, the brother of Jesus, who led the church in Jerusalem. He writes to "the twelve tribes scattered among the nations" (James 1:1), Jewish believers in Jesus who were often poor and often pushed around by wealthier neighbors. Just before our chapter he has warned them, "Do not merely listen to the word, and so deceive yourselves. Do what it says" (James 1:22). Then he paints two scenes so vivid you can almost smell the room.

In the first, a man walks into the church gathering "wearing a gold ring and fine clothes," and right behind him comes "a poor man in filthy old clothes" (James 2:2). The rich man is offered a good seat. The poor man is told, "You stand there" or "Sit on the floor by my feet" (James 2:3). James is blunt about this: "believers in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ must not show favoritism" (James 2:1). Then he moves to a second scene, quieter and somehow worse. A brother or sister arrives with no coat and nothing to eat, and a fellow believer smiles warmly and sends them off with a blessing.

"Suppose a brother or a sister is without clothes and daily food. If one of you says to them, 'Go in peace; keep warm and well fed,' but does nothing about their physical needs, what good is it? In the same way, faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead." (James 2:15–17)

"Go in peace" was an ordinary, gracious Jewish farewell, the kind of thing a kind person says at the door. Filipinos have our own versions: Ingat ka, God bless, ipagdadasal kita. The words are good. James's point is that the words, left alone, leave the sister exactly as cold and hungry as she was when she knocked. Her stomach cannot digest a blessing. James then asks whether "such faith" can save (James 2:14), and he answers with a word that sounds like a hospital chart: it is nekros, dead (James 2:17). He even observes that "even the demons believe" there is one God, and they shudder (James 2:19). Correct belief, on its own, describes a corpse with excellent information.

The turn that opens the whole chapter comes when James reaches for his two examples. He chooses Abraham, the revered father of the nation, who trusted God enough to offer his son Isaac, and Rahab, a Canaanite prostitute in Jericho who hid two Israelite spies and "sent them off in a different direction" (James 2:25). It is hard to imagine two people further apart in reputation, and James sets them side by side on purpose. About Abraham he writes, "You see that his faith and his actions were working together, and his faith was made complete by what he did" (James 2:22). The Greek verb for "working together" is synergei, the root of our word "synergy." Faith and action, in James's picture, are partners carried through the same gate at the same moment, much like the sugar and salt that cross the gut wall together and draw life in behind them.

This suggests a gentler way to read a chapter that many of us have read as a scolding. James never asks us to manufacture good deeds to earn God's favor; elsewhere the Bible is clear that we are saved by grace through faith (Ephesians 2:8–9), and Paul goes on in the very next verse to say we were created "to do good works" (Ephesians 2:10). James is describing what living faith naturally looks like when it is healthy. Abraham's trust was "made complete," brought to its intended end, when it moved his hands. Rahab's quiet belief that Israel's God was real became visible the night she let down a rope. Her faith was small, recent, and wrapped in a messy past, and James honors it alongside the patriarch's because it acted. And Abraham, he says, "was called God's friend" (James 2:23). Friendship with God is the warm center of this hard-sounding chapter.

Filipino homes already understand this in their own way. Many of us grew up with a nanay or lola who, at the first sign of a child's loose stomach, stirred a packet of Oresol into a glass of water, or boiled rice water with a pinch of salt. She did not lecture about electrolytes. She knew the cure, and she put it in the child's hand. Most believers today carry a great deal of saving knowledge: that God is good, that he sees the poor, that the church is a family. The question James presses on us is whether that knowledge ever leaves the drum and reaches the cup.

So think of the person in your life who is waiting outside the door with a real need. It might be a coworker who skips lunch to save money, a relative drowning in hospital bills, a neighbor's child who cannot afford school supplies, or the quiet person at church who always sits alone. Before today ends, you can do one specific thing for that person that costs you something: buy the meal, send the load, sit beside them, make the call. Pray for them too, and then let the prayer move your hands, because that is how James says faith is made complete.

Dilip Mahalanabis lived to see his simple mixture adopted around the world, and it is estimated to have saved tens of millions of lives. The knowledge had been true for years before 1971. It became life the day someone was willing to carry it to the people who were dying. Your faith is true as well, and Christ has given it to you as a gift. Faith that stays in the heart saves no one; faith becomes life the moment it is poured into someone's cup. Somewhere today, someone is holding out their hands, and you are the one God has placed close enough to fill them.

articles.title: The Painted Men on the Wall
articles.dek: In one of Ezekiel's hardest chapters, a nation falls in love with a picture. All the while, the One who had pitched his tent among them waits for her to come home.
articles.quote: Faithful love looks ordinary up close, because it is busy carving the steps you climb every day.
articles.body:
In the 1950s, in the hills of Jiangjin in China's Chongqing region, a young man named Liu Guojiang made a choice that set his whole village talking. He had fallen in love with Xu Chaoqing, a widow about ten years older than he was, who already had children of her own. The gossip grew so loud that the couple finally left the village and climbed into the mountains, where they made a simple home high on a steep slope, far from anyone's opinion.

The path down the mountain was dangerous, and Liu worried that his wife would slip whenever she went down for supplies. So he picked up a chisel and began cutting steps into the rock, and he kept cutting for the rest of his life. When a group of hikers came upon the elderly couple in 2001, the staircase had grown to more than six thousand steps, and Chinese newspapers began calling it the "Love Ladder." Liu died in 2007. The steps are still there, worn smooth by visitors who come to see what fifty years of ordinary faithfulness looks like when it is carved into stone.

Filipinos understand this kind of love, because so many of us were raised by it. We have seen it in a father who drove the same jeepney route for thirty years so his children could finish school, and in a lola who rose before dawn to cook rice for grandchildren who rarely thought to thank her. That kind of love seldom gets photographed, yet it is what holds a family together. Today's reading from Ezekiel is about a people who stopped seeing that kind of love because they had fallen for a picture on a wall.

Ezekiel was a priest carried off to Babylon with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC. He wrote to fellow exiles who still believed Jerusalem could never fall, since God's temple stood there. Chapter 23 is a parable, deliberately blunt and uncomfortable, about two sisters married to the Lord. "The older was named Oholah, and her sister was Oholibah," God says. "They were mine.... Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem" (Ezekiel 23:4).

The names hold a quiet heartbreak. Both are built on the Hebrew word ohel, meaning "tent," the same word used for the tabernacle where God met his people in the wilderness. Oholah can be read as "her tent," and Oholibah as "my tent is in her." Many scholars hear a contrast in those names: Samaria built her own shrines, while Jerusalem was the city where God had chosen to place his own dwelling. The younger sister was the one the Lord had come to live with.

The older sister went first. Oholah chased after Assyria, dazzled by soldiers "clothed in blue, governors and commanders, all of them handsome young men" (Ezekiel 23:6). In the language of the parable, the lovers she trusted became the ones who destroyed her, and history confirms it: Assyria crushed Samaria in 722 BC and scattered its people. Jerusalem watched it all happen from a few days' walk away. Then comes one of the saddest sentences in the chapter: "Her sister Oholibah saw this, yet in her lust and prostitution she was more depraved than her sister" (Ezekiel 23:11). She had seen the ending with her own eyes, and she walked the same road anyway. Then Ezekiel adds a strange and unforgettable detail.

"But she carried her prostitution still further. She saw men portrayed on a wall, figures of Chaldeans portrayed in red, with belts around their waists and flowing turbans on their heads; all of them looked like Babylonian chariot officers, natives of Chaldea. As soon as she saw them, she lusted after them and sent messengers to them in Chaldea." (Ezekiel 23:14–16)

The kings of Mesopotamia were famous for covering their palace walls with carved and painted scenes of officers, chariots, and conquests. Those images were advertising, meant to make an empire look strong, splendid, and irresistible. In the parable, Jerusalem falls in love with these men before she has ever met them. The "adultery" Ezekiel describes is spiritual and political: Judah's kings kept reaching for the protection of foreign powers, and with those alliances came foreign gods. Years earlier, King Hezekiah had proudly opened his storehouses to envoys from Babylon (2 Kings 20:12–15), and the infatuation never quite went away. Jerusalem fell in love with paint.

The next verse shows where that kind of love always leads. Once the Babylonians actually came, "after she had been defiled by them, she turned away from them in disgust" (Ezekiel 23:17). Then she went looking for Egypt again (Ezekiel 23:19–21). The pattern is painfully human. The heart moves from fascination to disappointment and then on to the next picture. A heart that lives on images can never be satisfied, because the image will always look better than the real person who has to show up on an ordinary Tuesday.

God names the real wound in a single verse: "Since you have forgotten me and turned your back on me..." (Ezekiel 23:35). The deepest sorrow of this chapter lies in the forgetting more than in the painting itself. The One whose tent was in her had been there all along, faithful and near, carving steps she no longer noticed. Chapter 24 carries the consequence. God tells Ezekiel to "record this date, this very date, because the king of Babylon has laid siege to Jerusalem this very day" (Ezekiel 24:2). The handsome officers from the wall had arrived, and this time they came as an army.

Ezekiel's book keeps going, though, and so does God's love. A few chapters later the same prophet hears the Lord promise, "I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit in you" (Ezekiel 36:26). The book closes with a renamed Jerusalem: "THE LORD IS THERE" (Ezekiel 48:35). God did not fold up his tent and leave for good. Centuries later John would write that "the Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us" (John 1:14), and the Greek verb there, eskēnōsen, literally means "pitched his tent." The God of Oholibah came back to live among his people in person, and the Bible's final pages picture a bride made ready and a voice announcing, "Look! God's dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them" (Revelation 21:3).

We all have painted walls now, and most of them fit in our pockets. A husband scrolls past curated lives and begins to find his wife plain. A wife measures her marriage against couples who post only their best angles. A friend drifts away from the barkada who stood with them through the hard years, drawn toward people who simply look more impressive. Even our walk with God can cool when his quiet presence seems dull beside the bright, loud things we keep looking at. The people who love us most faithfully often seem ordinary up close, because their love is made of steps cut patiently over many years.

This week, think of one person who has been carving steps for you, perhaps a parent, a spouse, an old friend, or a coworker who always covers for you without being asked, and tell them plainly what their faithfulness has meant to you. Then give the Lord the first few minutes of your morning before you open any screen, and thank him that his tent is still pitched where you are. Faithful love looks ordinary up close, because it is busy carving the steps you climb every day.

If you have spent years chasing painted figures, Ezekiel's story is no reason to despair. The God who grieved over Oholibah is the same God who promised her a new heart and came in person to bring her home. The staircase is already there, cut step by step at Calvary, and the One who carved it is waiting at the top for you.

articles.title: Awake Before the Watchman
articles.dek: The writer of Psalm 119 knew the long, grey hours before dawn. What he did with them can change the way you spend yours.
articles.quote: Whatever has drawn near to you in the night, the Lord has drawn near as well, and he is close enough to hear you whisper.
articles.body:
Anyone who has worked the graveyard shift at a call center in Makati or Cebu knows a particular hour. The last call is finished, the headset comes off, and you step out of the air-conditioned office into a city that has not yet woken up. The jeepneys are few. The streets are washed in a grey half-light that belongs to the night and the morning at once. On almost every corner, though, one window is already glowing. It is the panaderya, where the baker has been kneading dough since two o'clock so that the pandesal will be warm in its paper bag by the time the barangay opens its eyes.

There is a quiet fellowship among the people awake at that hour. The security guard nods at the nurse walking home from her rounds, and the tindera rolls up the steel shutter of her sari-sari store while the first tricycle sputters to life down the road. A young agent buys a dozen pandesal for a family that will still be asleep when she gets home, leaves the bag on the table with a short note, and finally lies down. Most of the country never sees this hour, yet a great deal of love quietly gets done in it. Filipinos know as well as anyone that the time before sunrise can hold weariness and tenderness side by side, along with worries that feel heavier in the dark.

The writer of Psalm 119 knew that hour too. His psalm is the longest chapter in the Bible, an acrostic poem of twenty-two stanzas in which every one of the eight lines in a stanza begins with the same letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Today's stanza belongs to the letter Qoph. We do not know the author's name, but the psalm lets us see his circumstances. He is under real pressure from powerful people. Earlier he writes, "Though rulers sit together and slander me, your servant will meditate on your decrees" (Psalm 119:23). He is a man being talked about behind closed doors, and he has learned to carry that weight to God.

In this stanza his prayer grows urgent. "I call with all my heart; answer me, LORD, and I will obey your decrees" (Psalm 119:145). Then, before the sun comes up, he is already at it: "I rise before dawn and cry for help; I have put my hope in your word. My eyes stay open through the watches of the night, that I may meditate on your promises" (Psalm 119:147–148).

The Hebrew behind those two verses carries a lovely detail that English struggles to keep. Both lines use the same verb, qadam, which means to go ahead of, to arrive early, to be there first. A very literal rendering of verse 147 would be "I came before the twilight," and of verse 148, "My eyes came before the night watches." In ancient Israel the night was divided into watches, shifts kept by the men who guarded the city walls (Judges 7:19 mentions "the middle watch"). The psalmist pictures himself awake before the guard changes, already at his post of prayer while the watchman is still rubbing his eyes. He is the baker of his household, up before everyone else, working something good into the dark hours so there will be bread when morning comes.

He is also honest about why he cannot sleep. In verse 150 he names the trouble outright, and then, in the very next line, he names Someone else.

"Those who devise wicked schemes are near, but they are far from your law. Yet you are near, LORD, and all your commands are true." (Psalm 119:150–151)

The same Hebrew word for "near" (qarob) appears in both verses, and the psalmist sets the two uses next to each other on purpose. The schemers have drawn close. They are near enough to plot, near enough to whisper, near enough to keep a man awake at three in the morning. He admits all of that plainly. Then he places a second nearness beside the first: the Lord is near as well. There is a gentle irony here too. The people who stand closest to him in the story are, by his own words, far from God's law, while the God who reigns above the heavens turns out to be the One standing closest of all.

This verse has a beautiful echo elsewhere in the Psalms. Psalm 145, a psalm of David, says, "The LORD is near to all who call on him, to all who call on him in truth" (Psalm 145:18). Set that beside our stanza and the pieces fit like a key in a lock. Our psalmist opened with "I call with all my heart" (Psalm 119:145). He ended up confessing, "Yet you are near, LORD, and all your commands are true" (Psalm 119:151). Calling, nearness and truth appear in both places. One way to read this is that the psalmist did in the dark exactly what David's song promises: he called, and in the calling he discovered that the Lord was already close.

That discovery did not come to him from nowhere. The stanza closes with a line about memory: "Long ago I learned from your statutes that you established them to last forever" (Psalm 119:152). What he learned in ordinary daylight, in years when life was calmer, became the thing that held him when the night grew long. The promises he had stored away earlier were waiting for him at the hour he most needed them, like bread a loving hand had left on the table.

Most of us have our own version of that hour. It may be the bill you cannot yet pay, or the message from a relative abroad that has gone strangely quiet. It may be a diagnosis, a child who has drifted, a supervisor whose words keep replaying in your mind. Worries have a way of moving closer after midnight, and in the dark they often seem larger than they will look at breakfast. The psalmist offers a way to spend those hours that is simple enough for a tired person to follow. He speaks honestly to God about what has come near, and then he deliberately turns his attention to the One who is nearer, holding on to a promise he learned long before.

You can prepare for your own night watches the way a baker prepares the dough the evening before. Choose one promise from Scripture this week, perhaps verse 151 itself, and write it on a small card you keep beside your bed or set it as the first thing you see when you check your phone. When you wake at an hour you did not choose, and the old worries crowd in, say it quietly to the Lord in the dark: "Yet you are near, LORD, and all your commands are true." You may find, as the psalmist did, that prayer offered before dawn has a way of reaching the morning ahead of you.

Another psalm reminds us that "he who watches over Israel will neither slumber nor sleep" (Psalm 121:4). The guards on Jerusalem's walls changed shifts through the night because every one of them grew tired, but the One who keeps watch over you has never needed relief. Whatever has drawn near to you in the night, the Lord has drawn near as well, and he is close enough to hear you whisper. So if you find yourself awake tonight, with the city silent and only the panaderya light glowing down the street, take heart. You are keeping watch in good company, and the morning he has prepared for you is already on its way.

articles.title: The General Who Waited on a Weatherman
articles.dek: On the eve of D-Day, the most powerful commander on earth put his trust in a quiet Scottish meteorologist. Proverbs 24 says that is exactly what strength looks like.
articles.quote: In the eyes of Scripture, strength is the humility to be steered.
articles.body:
On the night of June 4, 1944, rain lashed the windows of Southwick House, a country mansion near Portsmouth on the southern coast of England. Inside, General Dwight D. Eisenhower, Supreme Commander of the Allied forces, sat with his senior officers around a long table. More than 150,000 soldiers were waiting to cross the English Channel, along with thousands of ships and aircraft. Eisenhower had already postponed the invasion of Normandy by one day because of a violent storm, and the tides and moonlight would allow only a few more chances before the whole operation had to wait for weeks.

Every eye in the room turned to a tall, reserved Scotsman named James Stagg. He was a group captain in the Royal Air Force and the chief meteorologist for the invasion, a scientist who had spent his career studying the atmosphere rather than commanding troops. Using reports from ships and weather planes far out over the Atlantic, Stagg told the generals something no one expected: a brief break in the weather was coming, a narrow window of calmer skies on June 6, wedged between two storms. Eisenhower went around the table and asked each commander for his view. Then, after a long silence, he gave the order to go.

Across the Channel, German forecasters had no access to those Atlantic reports and saw only continuing storms. Several senior officers left their posts, and Field Marshal Erwin Rommel drove home to Germany for his wife's birthday. When the Allied ships appeared off the beaches of Normandy on the morning of June 6, the defenders were caught off guard. Historians still point to that forecast as one of the hinges of the war.

There is one more detail in the story that is easy to miss. Before the landings, Eisenhower quietly wrote a short note to be released if the invasion failed. It ended with these words: "If any blame or fault attaches to the attempt it is mine alone." The most powerful general in the world had leaned on the counsel of many people, including a weatherman most soldiers had never heard of, and he was prepared to carry the full weight of the outcome himself. That combination of listening and responsibility is precisely what a short passage in Proverbs 24 describes.

These verses belong to a section of Proverbs called "the sayings of the wise" (Proverbs 22:17), a collection of about thirty short teachings addressed to a young person being trained for life, and possibly for public service. Just before our passage, the writer has said that "by wisdom a house is built, and through understanding it is established" (Proverbs 24:3). Then he moves from the household to the battlefield, from building a home to defending one.

"The wise prevail through great power, and those who have knowledge muster their strength. Surely you need guidance to wage war, and victory is won through many advisers." (Proverbs 24:5–6, NIV)

The word translated "guidance" in verse 6 is the Hebrew tachbulot. Many scholars connect it with the word for a ship's rope and with the sailors who handled those ropes, so the picture behind it is the skill of steering a vessel. Guidance, in the Hebrew imagination, is what keeps a ship on course when wind and current pull in other directions. Proverbs uses the same word elsewhere when it says, "For lack of guidance a nation falls, but victory is won through many advisers" (Proverbs 11:14).

Read side by side, verses 5 and 6 offer a surprising definition of power. Verse 5 says the wise are strong, and verse 6 immediately explains where that strength comes from: from guidance and from many advisers. The strongest person in this passage is the one most willing to be counseled. In the eyes of Scripture, strength is the humility to be steered. A ship that refuses the pull of its ropes is simply drifting, however large it may be.

The verses that follow show the opposite kind of person. "Wisdom is too high for fools; in the assembly at the gate they must not open their mouths" (Proverbs 24:7). In ancient Israel, the city gate was where the elders sat to settle disputes and make decisions, as Boaz did when he arranged to marry Ruth (Ruth 4:1–2). The fool has nothing to offer in that place because he has never learned to listen, so wisdom stays out of his reach like fruit on a high branch. Verses 8 and 9 then describe the schemer who plots evil alone and the mocker who scoffs at anyone who might correct him, and both end up distrusted by the community. Proverbs makes the same point elsewhere: "The way of fools seems right to them, but the wise listen to advice" (Proverbs 12:15).

Most of us agree with all of this in principle and still find it hard to practice. Asking for counsel can feel like admitting weakness. Filipinos know the pull of hiya, the shame of looking like we cannot manage our own affairs, and the quiet pride of saying kaya ko 'to, "I can handle this." So we make large decisions about money, work abroad, marriage, or a struggling business in the privacy of our own heads, and we tell others only after the choice has been made.

This is where the gospel speaks with real tenderness. The good news of Jesus begins by telling us honestly that we are not sufficient in ourselves, and then it tells us that God loves us fully anyway. A person who has accepted that truth at the foot of the cross no longer needs to protect an image of self-sufficiency. Such a person is free to say "I need help" without feeling diminished, because their worth was settled by grace long before they asked anyone for advice.

The gospel also gives us the best Counselor of all. Isaiah, foretelling the coming Messiah, gave him the title "Wonderful Counselor" (Isaiah 9:6), and James promises that "if any of you lacks wisdom, you should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to you" (James 1:5). God does not scold us for asking. And where Eisenhower was prepared to accept blame for a decision that was his own, Jesus went further and took on blame that was never his: "He himself bore our sins in his body on the cross" (1 Peter 2:24). The Counselor who guides us is also the Savior who carries the weight of our worst mistakes.

In practical terms, Proverbs 24 invites us to build a small circle of trusted voices around the decisions that matter. The phrase "many advisers" suggests variety, people who will tell us what we would rather not hear, much as Stagg had to deliver the unwelcome news that the invasion must be delayed. A wise circle might include a mature believer, someone with practical experience in the area you are facing, and someone who simply knows you well enough to see your blind spots. If a decision is weighing on you this week, you could take one concrete step: pray about it honestly, then write down the names of two people whose judgment you respect and ask them to sit with you over coffee and speak freely.

Eisenhower's courage on the night of June 4 is remembered because he gave the order to go. The deeper lesson is that his order rested on the voices he chose to hear. May you find that same quiet strength today, the kind that listens before it moves, leans on the Wonderful Counselor, and rests in the One who has already carried the blame on your behalf.
